main_point: Courts should start the limitations clock for software defects at the manufacturer's public patch note, because owners can't see code.

look_for.item: The strongest counterargument, stated fairly and answered
look_for.note: The roadmap promises objections; none are addressed.

look_for.item: Premises the argument needs but never states (normative commitments, empirical assumptions, a baseline)
look_for.quote: Tying accrual to disclosure rewards them for telling owners promptly.
look_for.note: Assumes manufacturers will disclose, and disclose accurately. Never stated or defended.

look_for.item: Claims worded more strongly than the support on the page
look_for.note: Asserted without addressing vague, partial, or buried patch notes.

look_for.item: The step from description to prescription, and whether the draft justifies it
look_for.quote: When the product can change after the sale, asking when the owner should have discovered the defect is asking the wrong question.
look_for.note: The move from the fixed-product premise to a new accrual rule is motivated.

look_for.item: Hard cases or examples that test the proposal
look_for.quote: The rule would not displace the discovery rule for defects that owners can find without help.
look_for.note: No example of a vague patch note, a defect never disclosed, or a defect fixed silently.

look_for.item: Consistency across Parts in definitions, the scope of the claim, and the standard applied
look_for.quote: Courts should consider the timing of a manufacturer's patch disclosures, among other factors, in deciding when a software claim accrues.
look_for.note: 'Latent' shifts meaning between Parts I and III, and the conclusion shifts from a rule to a factor.

findings.quote: Third, the rule puts the burden on the party with the information. Manufacturers know when they have found and fixed a defect. Tying accrual to disclosure rewards them for telling owners promptly.
findings.issue: The rule gives manufacturers a reason to delay or bury disclosure, and the draft claims the opposite
findings.why_it_matters: This is the first objection a commentator will raise. As written, the third advantage reads as if the author hasn't noticed that the defendant now controls when the clock starts.

findings.issue: The promised objections Part is missing
findings.why_it_matters: A reader who trusts the roadmap will look for answers that aren't there, and that missing Part is where the incentive problem has to be met.

findings.quote: the limitations period should begin to run no earlier than the date on which the manufacturer publicly discloses the defect
findings.issue: No answer for defects that are never disclosed or are fixed silently
findings.why_it_matters: 'No earlier than' disclosure implies the clock may never start for an undisclosed defect. A skeptic will press on whether that's intended.

findings.quote: A defect is latent, in the language of these cases, when the manufacturer could not have known of it at the time of sale.
findings.issue: 'Latent' changes meaning between Part I and Part III
findings.why_it_matters: Part III uses 'latent defect' for a defect the owner can't see. A careful reader will notice the shift and ask which standard the rule uses.

findings.quote: Courts should consider the timing of a manufacturer's patch disclosures, among other factors, in deciding when a software claim accrues.
findings.issue: The conclusion retreats from a rule to a factor
findings.why_it_matters: A skeptic attacks whichever version is weaker; stating two versions invites the charge that the author isn't sure.

what_works.quote: The patch-notice rule applies only where the defect lives in code that the owner cannot see.
what_works.note: A clear limit. Narrowing the claim this way makes it easier to defend.

related_work.work: Law-and-economics work on disclosure incentives and strategic delay
related_work.why: The incentive objection has a literature. Engaging it would show the author has seen the problem.
